title: The RSS Just Called for Dialogue With Pakistan. That Sentence Alone Tells You How Much Has Changed.
excerpt: Dattatreya Hosabale's remarks to PTI have triggered reactions from Islamabad to Jammu to the Congress war room. For the diaspora, it reopens the most emotional question in South Asian geopolitics.
body:
In an interview with the Press Trust of India earlier this month, Dattatreya Hosabale — the Sarkaryavah and effective number two of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh — said something that would have been unremarkable from a Congress leader or a retired diplomat. From the RSS, it landed like a thunderclap.

India, Hosabale said, should persist with attempts at dialogue with Pakistan. The door for people-to-people contact should remain open. Trade, visas, and cultural exchange should continue even as India maintains firm security measures. And then he went further: India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, he argued, constitute one nation — differentiated as nation-states but bound by "common ancestry and DNA."

The reactions were immediate, wide-ranging, and often contradictory — which is precisely what makes the remarks significant.

## The Timing Is Everything

Hosabale's intervention did not arrive in a vacuum. India severed diplomatic ties with Pakistan in the aftermath of the Pahalgam terror attack. The Indus Water Treaty stands suspended. There are no official exchanges, no back-channel conversations that anyone will acknowledge, and no cricket. Pakistani cricketers remain barred from the IPL, and even the purchase of a Bangladeshi player by an IPL franchise recently triggered protests.

Against this backdrop, the RSS — the ideological mothership of the ruling BJP — calling for dialogue is not a policy recommendation. It is a political signal. The question is: to whom?

Diplomatic observers are divided. Some see a trial balloon, floated with the tacit approval of the Prime Minister's Office to test public appetite for a reset. Others view it as the RSS reasserting its ideological independence from the government, a reminder that the Sangh's vision of Akhand Bharat — an undivided civilisational India — sometimes requires engagement, not just confrontation.

## The Political Reactions

Congress MP Jairam Ramesh wasted no time. In a post on X, he sought to link the remarks to another RSS functionary, Ram Madhav, who had recently visited the United States and apologised for claiming that India stopped buying Iranian oil at Washington's request. Ramesh's implication: the RSS was softening its Pakistan stance under American pressure, a charge the Sangh has historically found insulting.

From Srinagar, the response was more welcoming. PDP president Mehbooba Mufti publicly backed Hosabale's call, urging Prime Minister Modi to initiate talks and referencing Atal Bihari Vajpayee's earlier outreach. For Kashmiri political leaders, any opening toward dialogue is a lifeline — their region bears the heaviest cost of the frozen relationship.

India's former Chief of Army Staff also weighed in, though more cautiously. The military establishment has historically been sceptical of civilian diplomatic overtures toward Pakistan, arguing that every previous peace process was eventually derailed by a terror attack.

Sharat Sabharwal, India's former ambassador to Pakistan, offered the most measured assessment. "India should manage its difficult relationship with Pakistan using all instruments at its disposal — deterrence, coercion and diplomacy — as required," he wrote on X. "Why should it remain deprived altogether of one instrument?"

## The One-Nation Thesis

The most provocative element of Hosabale's remarks was not his call for dialogue — it was his framework. By arguing that India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh constitute "one nation" bound by common ancestry, he invoked the RSS's foundational concept of civilisational unity while simultaneously undermining the very basis of Pakistan's existence as a separate state.

Diplomatic observers have called this argument vague at best and counterproductive at worst. The idea that Pakistan would welcome being told it is not really a separate nation, even in cultural terms, misreads Islamabad's political psychology. And it complicates the very dialogue Hosabale claims to seek: you cannot negotiate with a country whose sovereignty you have just philosophically denied.

Yet within the RSS worldview, this is not a contradiction. The Sangh has always drawn a distinction between the nation-state (a political and legal entity) and the nation (a civilisational and cultural one). Hosabale was not questioning Pakistan's sovereignty — he was asserting that the people on both sides of the border share a deeper bond than their governments acknowledge.

## What the Diaspora Hears

For NRIs, the India-Pakistan question is never merely geopolitical. It is personal. Millions of Indian-Americans, British Indians, and Canadian Indians trace their ancestral roots to regions divided by Partition — Punjab, Sindh, Bengal. Family histories of displacement, loss, and reinvention are woven into the fabric of diaspora identity.

Hosabale's remarks reopen a wound that never fully closes: whether engagement or isolation better serves the cause of peace. Older NRIs who remember the Vajpayee-Musharraf thaw tend to favour dialogue. Younger diaspora members, shaped by the post-Pulwama and post-Pahalgam anger, are more hawkish. The RSS's internal debate mirrors the diaspora's own.

His reference to "common ancestry and DNA" also resonates in diaspora spaces where South Asians of all backgrounds — Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi — live, work, and socialise together. The geopolitical hostility between their home countries sits uneasily alongside the cultural intimacy of their daily lives.

## Where This Goes

The BJP has remained notably silent on Hosabale's remarks. No senior party leader has endorsed them. No one has repudiated them either. This calculated ambiguity is itself a signal: the ruling party is watching to see how the public reacts before committing to a position.

Whether Hosabale's call for dialogue leads to any concrete change in policy is, for now, unknowable. What is clear is that the ground has shifted. When the RSS — the organisation that shaped the ideological framework for India's hardline Pakistan policy — calls for keeping the window open, it suggests that even within the Sangh Parivar, the question of Pakistan is being reassessed.

The door to dialogue, it seems, is not yet open. But someone very senior has just rattled the lock.
